links.outcome: Physician intent to act on LLM abstracts containing false claims; discrimination of true vs false
links.effect: Physicians would act on 68% (54/80) of abstracts; sensitivity 78%, specificity 43%; positive likelihood ratio 1.35 (95% CI 0.98-1.85); true and false abstracts rated similarly for perceived accuracy (P=.21).
links.quote: Overall, physicians reported that they would act on 68% (54/80) of abstracts.

links.outcome: Whether physicians detect incorrect AI-generated content and overreliance on polished outputs
links.effect: Specificity of decision to act was 43% (17/40); true and false abstracts rated similarly on accuracy (3.15 vs 2.88; P=.21); perceived accuracy, precision, and structure strongly associated with intended action (all P<.001).
links.quote: Physicians frequently reported an intent to act on LLM-generated abstracts containing false claims, and true and false abstracts were not reliably distinguished on perceived quality measures.

screen.reason: The study tests physicians' ability to detect fabricated medical claims in LLM-generated scientific abstracts via a vignette-based study, evaluating clinician susceptibility to AI hallucination without testing an organizational deployment safeguard.
